claims.text: The dual-phase FCC/BCC coating has superior creep resistance relative to comparable single-phase coatings.
The superior creep resistance arises from nanoscopic, coherent FCC/BCC phase boundaries.
The as-deposited coating contains an interpenetrating dual-phase microstructure of FCC and BCC grains.
The FCC and BCC grains have well-defined, coherent interfaces.
Coherent FCC/BCC interfaces impede dislocation motion during sustained loading.
Coherent FCC/BCC interfaces act as barriers to dislocation climb.
Coherent FCC/BCC interfaces act as barriers to dislocation cross-slip.
Nanoscale phase boundaries interrupt the continuity of slip systems.
Restricting dislocation motion reduces the rate at which plastic deformation accumulates under sustained load.
At elevated temperature under sustained stress, dual-phase coatings will have lower creep strain rates than predominantly single-phase coatings of the same overall composition.
At elevated temperature under sustained stress, dual-phase coatings will exhibit a delayed onset of plastic deformation relative to predominantly single-phase coatings.
The proposed interface-mediated mechanism is effective at stresses below the yield limit.
The proposed mechanism operates at temperatures high enough to activate creep but below those causing phase instability or excessive diffusion.
Dislocation pile-ups should be observable near FCC/BCC phase boundaries if those boundaries critically impede dislocation motion.
